soil-found-064.title: From granite and basalt to soil: weathering's ledger
soil-found-064.text: Turning rock into soil takes between 100 and 1,000 years, a brief interval in geologic time. In that span, weathering turns the minerals of rock into {{ref:soil-chem-079}} and the minerals of {{ref:soil-chem-163}}. Granite shows the sequence. Hornblende goes first. The dark sheet mineral of {{ref:soil-form-144}} then alters to another sheet mineral, and oligoclase and microcline go last. All end as clay and oxides of iron. The chemistry shifts with them. Compared with the bedrock, soil from granite loses calcium, sodium and ferrous iron, 40% of its magnesium and 15% of its silicon. It gains at least 50% in aluminum and potassium, triples its titanium and raises its ferric iron by an order of magnitude. Basalt weathers more easily than granite. It formed hotter and drier, and it is fine-grained and glassy. It turns to potassium-poor {{ref:soil-chem-093}}, then to {{ref:soil-chem-088}}. Climate writes the ending. Continuous intense washing by rain, as in rain forests, ends in the aluminum ore of {{ref:soil-chem-108}}. Intense but seasonal monsoon rain ends in an iron- and titanium-rich material, {{ref:soil-form-065}}. Geologists track the progress with the chemical index of alteration, 100 Al2O3/(Al2O3 + CaO + Na2O + K2O). It runs from 47 for unweathered upper crust rock to 100 for fully weathered material.
